Chapter 4 · History · India and the Contemporary World II

The Age of Industrialisation

Industry did not begin with the factory. This chapter follows the slow growth of proto-industrialisation, the industrial revolution in Britain, the fate of the Indian weaver under the Company, and the rise of Indian mills to the First World War.

Chapter Overview

What this chapter is about, at a glance

The chapter begins before the factory. In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, merchants from European towns began employing peasants and artisans within the villages — supplying raw material, paying for the work and selling the product — a system historians call proto-industrialisation. It was a decentralised, hand-based industrial production for an international market, and it grew outside the control of the urban guilds.

The industrial revolution then produced the factory. In Britain a series of inventions — the Spinning Jenny (1764), the water frame and cotton mill of Richard Arkwright (1771), James Watt’s steam engine (1781) and Cartwright’s power loom (1785) — transformed cotton textiles, and the steam engine and railways transformed transport. Yet hand labour survived long after machines: industrialists preferred hand labour where wages were low and demand was for variety, and workers resisted machines — women in England attacked the Spinning Jenny, and the Luddites destroyed frames.

In India, the Company first intervened in the market through gomasthas — agents who supervised weavers, gave them loans and fixed prices — and the weavers’ position deteriorated as their bargaining power was destroyed. The first cotton mill came up in Bombay in 1854, and by 1874 the industry had spread to Bengal, Kanpur, Ahmedabad and Madras. Indian industrialists — Dwarkanath Tagore, Seth Hukumchand, the Tatas and Birlas — built mills and factories, and the First World War gave Indian industry its great opportunity, as British imports fell and Indian mills supplied the war effort.

The chapter closes with advertisements and labels — calendars, images of gods and emperors — through which manufacturers sought to create new consumers and national identity.

Proto-industrialisation

A phase of decentralised, hand-based industrial production for an international market, carried on in villages outside guild control.

Guild

An association of craftsmen and merchants that controlled production, prices and entry into a trade in a town.

Spinning Jenny

James Hargreaves’s machine of 1764 that speeded up spinning by allowing a single wheel to turn many spindles.

Water frame

Richard Arkwright’s water-powered spinning machine, used in his cotton mill of 1771.

Power loom

Edmund Cartwright’s loom of 1785, driven by power rather than by hand.

Gomastha

An Indian agent appointed by the East India Company to supervise weavers, collect supplies and examine cloth.

Sepoy

An Indian soldier in the Company’s army; the revolt of 1857 disrupted Indian markets and trade.

Jobber

A person employed by Indian mill owners to recruit new workers from villages; he began as a worker and used his influence to get people jobs.

Fly shuttle

A device that speeded up weaving; its spread in India increased the demand for cloth and expanded production.

First World War boom

The war of 1914–18 cut off British imports, and Indian mills supplied war needs, so industrial production in India rose sharply.

Before the Industrial Revolution — Proto-industrialisation

The industrial revolution did not begin from nothing. In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, merchants from the towns of Europe began moving to the countryside and supplying money to peasants and artisans, persuading them to produce for an international market. With the expansion of world trade and the acquisition of colonies, the demand for goods increased, and the urban crafts and trade guilds were unable to meet it — they were powerful associations that controlled production, prices and entry into the trade, and they restricted competition. So merchants turned to the countryside, where poor peasants and artisans were eager to work for money.

Definition

Proto-industrialisation — a phase of industrial production before factories, in which merchants controlled production in the countryside, supplying raw material to peasants and artisans who worked in their own homes, and selling the finished goods in the international market. It was decentralised and hand-based, but it was production for the world market.

This system had consequences. In the countryside, a close relationship developed between the town and the countryside: the merchants of the town supplied raw material and marketed the product, while the peasants and artisans worked at home. The proto-industrial system was thus controlled by merchants and not by the producers, and the producers became dependent on the merchants for work and wages.

The Coming of the Factory — Inventions and the Cotton Boom

The factory system grew out of a series of inventions in the cotton textile industry, where the demand for cheap, standard cloth was greatest.

The inventions that made the factory
InventionInventor and yearWhat it did
Spinning JennyJames Hargreaves, 1764Allowed a single wheel to turn many spindles, speeding up spinning dramatically
Water frameRichard Arkwright, 1769; cotton mill 1771Water-powered spinning; brought production into the mill
Steam engineJames Watt, 1781 (improved)Provided power independent of water, so mills could be built anywhere
Power loomEdmund Cartwright, 1785Mechanised weaving, completing the factory system in cotton
Cotton ginEli Whitney, 1793Separated cotton fibre from seed quickly, increasing the supply of raw cotton

The result was a cotton boom: British cotton production rose sharply, Manchester became the centre of the industry, and by the early nineteenth century cotton goods dominated British exports. The steam engine and railways then transformed transport — the first railway opened in 1830 — carrying coal, cotton and finished goods quickly and cheaply.

Why hand labour survived

Yet machines did not immediately replace hand labour. In Victorian Britain there was no shortage of human labour — poor peasants and vagrants moved to the towns in large numbers looking for work, and industrialists had no problem of labour shortage or high wages. Where wages were low, they preferred hand labour to machines, which were expensive. In industries with a seasonal demand, such as gas works and shipbuilding, hand labour was preferred because machines would be idle for part of the year. And in many trades demand was for a variety of designs and colours — hand-made goods could be varied, while machines produced standardised articles. So hand labour remained widespread well into the nineteenth century, and in some trades it survived into the twentieth.

Workers resist machines

Workers were not passive. In England, women who survived on hand spinning attacked the Spinning Jenny, because it threatened their livelihood — a crowd of women in a village near Blackburn destroyed the machines of a manufacturer. In the 1830s and 1840s, the “Luddites” — skilled workers in the woollen and cotton industry — destroyed frames and power looms, believing that machines would take away their jobs. The government responded with severe repression, and machine-breaking was made a capital offence. But the resistance was not simply technophobia: workers were defending their skills, their wages and their place in production.

The Workers and the Towns

The factory system created a new kind of working life. Work was now regulated by the clock: workers had to keep pace with machines, and the working day was long — twelve to sixteen hours in the early mills. Wages were low, and much of the work was done by women and children, who could be paid less and were thought to be more docile.

The towns that grew around the mills were crowded and unhealthy. Workers lived in back-to-back houses with no sanitation, and epidemics were common. Housing was provided by the employers in many cases, but at a rent, and the quality was poor. Reform came slowly — through Factory Acts limiting hours and the employment of children, and through the Chartist movement, which demanded political rights for working men.

Workers also organised. Trade unions were formed to bargain over wages and conditions, and strikes became a common form of protest. The “mill girls” of the textile towns and the skilled artisans of the older trades were among the first to organise.

India and the Company — Weavers, Gomasthas and Decline

Before the British, Indian cotton and silk textiles were among the most sought-after goods in the world. Surat on the west coast was a great port, and Indian cloth was exported to Europe, Africa and Asia. The English East India Company entered this trade in the seventeenth century, and by the eighteenth century it had become a territorial power.

The gomasthas

To obtain regular supplies of cloth, the Company appointed gomasthas — Indian agents who supervised weavers, collected supplies and examined the cloth. They gave loans to weavers to install looms, and in return the weavers were bound to sell only to the Company at a price fixed by it. The gomasthas were outsiders, with no long-term social link with the weaving villages, and they acted arrogantly and punished weavers for delays in supply.

The weavers lost their bargaining power. Earlier they could sell to several buyers and bargain over prices; now they were tied to the Company. Weavers who had taken loans could not sell to anyone else, and those who tried were punished. Many weavers deserted the villages and moved to other places, and some took to agriculture. The Company’s control over the weavers, together with the import of cheap British cloth, ruined the Indian textile industry.

Decline and the nineteenth century

By the end of the eighteenth century, the port of Surat declined as the Company shifted its operations to Bombay, Calcutta and Madras. British cloth, produced in mills, entered India in large quantities, and Indian weavers could not compete with its cheapness. The revolt of 1857 further disrupted markets and trade, and the weavers’ distress deepened.

The Growth of Indian Industry

Indian industry began to grow in the second half of the nineteenth century. The first cotton mill in India was set up in Bombay in 1854, followed by mills in Bengal (1855), Kanpur (1860s), Ahmedabad (1861) and Madras (1874). By the end of the century there were hundreds of mills, and India had become a major producer of cotton yarn and cloth.

Early Indian industrialists
IndustrialistContribution
Cowasjee NanabhoySet up the first cotton mill in Bombay in 1854
Dwarkanath TagorePioneer of Indian industry in Bengal; founded the Bengal Chamber of Commerce
Seth HukumchandSet up the first Indian jute mill in Calcutta in 1917
Jamsetji TataFounded the Tata Iron and Steel Company in 1907, with the plant at Jamshedpur from 1912
G.D. BirlaBuilt a large industrial empire in textiles, jute and other trades
Dinshaw Petit, Jamsetjee Nusserwanjee TataEarly mill owners and merchants of Bombay

Indian industrialists faced a difficult environment: British goods had free entry into India, while Indian goods faced tariffs in Britain; the colonial government was unsympathetic; and capital and technology had to be imported. They also had to create a market among Indian consumers who were used to hand-made cloth, which is why advertisements and labels became so important.

The First World War

The First World War (1914–18) transformed the situation. British industries were busy with war production, so Manchester imports into India declined; Indian mills were called upon to supply war needs — jute bags, cloth, boots — and the demand for Indian industrial goods rose. New factories and workshops were set up, and industrial production in India increased substantially. After the war, Manchester never recovered its old position in the Indian market, and Indian industry emerged stronger.

Workers in Indian mills

Indian mill owners recruited workers through jobbers — a jobber was an old worker who had influence in the villages and was sent to bring new recruits. He got a commission for each worker he brought, and he kept control over the workers once they arrived: he decided who worked on which machine and could extract money from them. The jobber thus became a powerful intermediary between the mill owner and the workers. Working conditions were harsh — long hours, low wages, no security — and workers lived in crowded chawls in Bombay, often returning to their villages at harvest time, which is why the workforce was seasonal and unstable.

Advertisements, Labels and the Making of Consumers

Industrialists had to persuade people to buy machine-made goods, and advertising became the means. From the late nineteenth century, Indian manufacturers used calendars, labels, posters and newspapers to advertise their products. Advertisements appeared on calendars, which hung in offices and homes all year, and on the labels of cloth and other goods.

The images were carefully chosen. Manufacturers used images of gods and goddesses — for example, a label showing God Vishnu — to give their products an aura of divinity and trust; they used royal and imperial imagery, such as the figure of a queen or an emperor, to suggest quality and status; and they used images of Indian women in traditional dress to suggest purity and Indianness. Manchester manufacturers, by contrast, used images of their own cities and factories, or of exotic “oriental” scenes, to sell their cloth in India.

Advertisements thus did two things at once: they created new consumers for goods that had not existed before, and they helped to shape a sense of national identity, as Indian manufacturers appealed to swadeshi sentiment and presented their goods as Indian against the foreign.

NCERT In-text Questions and Answers

The questions printed inside the chapter

These are the “Can you…” and activity questions that appear inside the chapter text. Model answers are based on the chapter itself.

1.

Explain why women workers in Britain attacked the Spinning Jenny.

Model answer

Because the Spinning Jenny threatened their livelihood. Many women survived by hand spinning, and the new machine allowed one worker to turn many spindles, so far fewer hands were needed. In a village near Blackburn a crowd of women destroyed the machines of a manufacturer — an attack on the machine that had taken away their work and wages.

2.

Explain why in the seventeenth century merchants from towns in Europe began employing peasants and artisans within the villages.

Model answer

Because the demand for goods had expanded with world trade and the colonies, and the urban guilds — which controlled production, prices and entry into trades — could not or would not expand output. Merchants therefore turned to the countryside, where poor peasants and artisans were willing to work for money, and organised production in their homes, supplying raw material and marketing the finished goods. This was proto-industrialisation.

3.

Explain why the port of Surat declined by the end of the eighteenth century.

Model answer

Because the English East India Company shifted its operations to Bombay, Calcutta and Madras, and because the Company’s control over weavers through gomasthas, together with the import of cheap British machine-made cloth, ruined the textile trade that Surat had lived on. Political instability and the decline of the Mughal order added to its troubles.

4.

Explain why the East India Company appointed gomasthas to supervise weavers in India.

Model answer

Because the Company needed regular, reliable supplies of cloth of consistent quality for export. The gomasthas supervised the weavers, collected the cloth, examined it and fixed the price; they gave loans for looms, which bound the weavers to sell only to the Company. The system eliminated Indian traders and middlemen and gave the Company control over production and price.

5.

Write the three features of the jobber.

Model answer

(i) He was an old worker who had influence in the villages and was employed by the mill owner to recruit new workers. (ii) He got a commission for each worker he brought, and once the workers arrived he decided who worked on which machine. (iii) He extracted money from the workers and controlled them, becoming a powerful intermediary between the owner and the workforce.

6.

Explain what is meant by proto-industrialisation.

Model answer

It refers to the phase of industrial production before factories, in which merchants controlled production in the countryside, supplying raw material to peasants and artisans who worked in their own homes, and selling the finished goods in the international market. It was decentralised and hand-based, but it was production for the world market — a “first” industrialisation that prepared the way for the factory.

7.

Why did some industrialists in nineteenth-century Europe prefer hand labour over machines?

Model answer

Because labour was abundant and cheap, so machines — which were expensive — were not always profitable; because in seasonal industries machines would lie idle for part of the year; and because many markets demanded a variety of designs and colours which hand production could supply but standardised machines could not. In Victorian Britain there was no shortage of workers, so the pressure to mechanise was weaker than in later periods.

8.

How did the East India Company procure regular supplies of cotton and silk textiles from Indian weavers?

Model answer

Through the gomastha system. The Company appointed Indian agents — gomasthas — who supervised the weavers, collected their cloth, examined its quality and fixed the price. The gomasthas gave loans to weavers to install looms, and in return the weavers were bound to sell only to the Company. Weavers who had taken loans could not sell to other buyers, and those who tried were punished; the Company also eliminated the Indian traders who had earlier competed for the cloth.

9.

Why did industrial production in India increase during the First World War?

Model answer

Because British industries were fully occupied with war production, so Manchester’s exports to India declined sharply, leaving the Indian market to Indian mills. Indian mills were also called upon to supply war needs — jute bags, cloth, boots and other goods — and new factories and workshops were set up. The result was a substantial rise in Indian industrial production, and after the war Manchester never regained its old position in the Indian market.

10.

Imagine you have been asked to write an article for an encyclopaedia on Britain and the history of cotton. Write your piece using information from the entire chapter.

Model answer

Model article: “Cotton was the first industry to be transformed by machinery. Before the factory, merchants organised production in the countryside — proto-industrialisation — but from the 1760s a series of inventions changed everything: Hargreaves’s Spinning Jenny (1764), Arkwright’s water-powered mill (1771), Watt’s steam engine (1781) and Cartwright’s power loom (1785). Manchester became the centre of the trade, and by the early nineteenth century cotton goods dominated British exports. Machines did not displace hand labour at once: where wages were low, demand seasonal or varied, employers preferred hand work, and workers resisted — women attacked the Spinning Jenny and the Luddites destroyed frames. The factory created long hours, low wages and crowded towns, and it also created trade unions, Factory Acts and Chartism. For India, British cotton meant the ruin of its weavers under the gomastha system — until Indian mills of their own arose from 1854 and seized their opportunity in the First World War.” (Student answers will vary.)

Important Questions and Answers

Board-style practice

Practice questions

Written in the style of CBSE board papers. They are additional practice, not NCERT originals.

1.

What is proto-industrialisation? Explain its features and significance. (5 marks)

Model answer

Proto-industrialisation was the phase of industrial production before factories. In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, as world trade and colonial demand grew, merchants from European towns began supplying money and raw material to peasants and artisans in the countryside, who produced goods in their own homes for an international market. Its features were: production was decentralised — carried on in villages and homes rather than in factories; it was hand-based, using traditional tools; it was controlled by merchants, who supplied the material and marketed the product; and it grew outside the control of the urban guilds, which had restricted production, prices and entry into trades. Its significance is that it prepared the ground for the factory system: it created a workforce accustomed to producing for distant markets, a merchant class with capital and commercial networks, and a supply of goods that the guilds could not have produced.

2.

Describe the inventions that created the factory system in Britain. (5 marks)

Model answer

The cotton industry was transformed by a series of inventions. The Spinning Jenny, invented by James Hargreaves in 1764, allowed a single wheel to turn many spindles and speeded up spinning dramatically. Richard Arkwright’s water frame, used in his cotton mill of 1771, harnessed water power and brought spinning into the factory. James Watt’s improved steam engine of 1781 provided power independent of water, so mills could be built anywhere. Edmund Cartwright’s power loom of 1785 mechanised weaving. Eli Whitney’s cotton gin of 1793 separated fibre from seed quickly, increasing the supply of raw cotton. Together these raised output enormously, made Manchester the centre of the trade, and by the early nineteenth century made cotton goods Britain’s leading export — while the steam engine and the railways (1830) transformed transport.

3.

Why did hand labour survive in nineteenth-century Britain? (5 marks)

Model answer

Because machines were not always profitable. In Victorian Britain there was no shortage of human labour: poor peasants and vagrants moved into the towns in large numbers looking for work, so wages were low and there was no pressure to replace workers with expensive machines. In seasonal industries such as gas works and shipbuilding, machines would lie idle for part of the year, so hand labour was preferred. In many trades, demand was for a variety of designs and colours, which hand production could supply but standardised machines could not. And workers themselves resisted: women attacked the Spinning Jenny and the Luddites destroyed frames and power looms, so employers sometimes avoided machines to prevent conflict.

4.

How did the Company’s gomastha system ruin the Indian weaver? (5 marks)

Model answer

The Company appointed gomasthas to supervise weavers, collect supplies and examine cloth, and to fix the price at which the Company would buy. The gomasthas gave loans to weavers for looms, but in return the weavers were bound to sell only to the Company. This destroyed the weavers’ bargaining power: earlier they could sell to several buyers and negotiate a price, now they had one buyer and a fixed price. The gomasthas were outsiders with no social ties to the weaving villages and behaved arrogantly, punishing weavers for delays. Weavers who took loans could not sell elsewhere, and those who tried were punished; many deserted their villages and some took to agriculture. Together with the flood of cheap British machine-made cloth, the system ruined the Indian textile industry and the port of Surat declined.

5.

Trace the growth of Indian industry from 1854 to 1918. (5 marks)

Model answer

The first cotton mill was set up in Bombay in 1854, followed by mills in Bengal (1855), Kanpur (1860s), Ahmedabad (1861) and Madras (1874). Indian industrialists — Cowasjee Nanabhoy, Dwarkanath Tagore, Dinshaw Petit, Jamsetjee Tata, Seth Hukumchand, G.D. Birla and Jamsetji Tata — built mills, jute factories and, from 1907, the Tata Iron and Steel Company with its plant at Jamshedpur from 1912. They worked against severe odds: British goods entered India freely while Indian goods faced tariffs abroad, the colonial government was unsympathetic, and capital and technology had to be imported. The turning point was the First World War: British industry was busy with war production, Manchester’s exports to India fell, Indian mills supplied war needs, and industrial production rose substantially — and Manchester never regained its position afterwards.

6.

How did advertisements and labels create new consumers in India? (5 marks)

Model answer

Industrialists had to persuade people used to hand-made cloth to buy machine-made goods, so from the late nineteenth century they used calendars, labels, posters and newspapers to advertise. Calendars were particularly effective because they hung in homes and offices all year. The images were carefully chosen: gods and goddesses gave products an aura of divinity and trust; royal and imperial figures suggested quality and status; images of Indian women in traditional dress suggested purity and Indianness. Manchester manufacturers used images of their own cities and factories, or exotic “oriental” scenes. Advertising thus did two things: it created markets for goods that had not existed before, and it helped shape a sense of national identity, as Indian manufacturers appealed to swadeshi sentiment.

7.

What were the working conditions of early factory workers in Britain? (3 marks)

Model answer

Long hours of twelve to sixteen a day, low wages, and work regulated by the clock and the pace of machines; large numbers of women and children were employed because they could be paid less. Workers lived in crowded back-to-back houses without sanitation, and epidemics were common. Reform came slowly through Factory Acts and through organisation in trade unions and the Chartist movement.

8.

Why did workers resist machines in Britain? (3 marks)

Model answer

Because machines threatened their skills, wages and employment. Women who survived by hand spinning attacked the Spinning Jenny; the Luddites destroyed frames and power looms in the 1830s and 1840s, believing machines would take their jobs. The government replied with severe repression, making machine-breaking a capital offence — but the resistance was a defence of livelihood, not mere fear of technology.

9.

What was the role of the jobber in Indian mills? (3 marks)

Model answer

The jobber was an old worker with influence in the villages whom the mill owner employed to recruit new workers. He received a commission for each recruit, decided who worked on which machine, and extracted money from the workers — becoming a powerful intermediary between owner and workforce.

10

Previous Year Questions (PYQs)

Asked in CBSE board exams

Previous year questions

These follow the pattern of questions set in CBSE Social Science papers for this chapter. Answers are model answers.

1.
CBSE pattern

Explain the term proto-industrialisation. (CBSE pattern, 2 marks)

Model answer

It refers to the phase of decentralised, hand-based industrial production for an international market before factories, in which merchants supplied raw material to peasants and artisans working in their homes and sold the finished goods.

2.
CBSE pattern

Who were gomasthas? What was their role? (3 marks)

Model answer

Gomasthas were Indian agents appointed by the East India Company to supervise weavers, collect supplies and examine cloth, and to fix prices. They gave loans for looms which bound weavers to sell only to the Company, and they punished weavers for delays.

3.
CBSE pattern

Why did women in Britain attack the Spinning Jenny? (2 marks)

Model answer

Because it threatened their livelihood: many women survived by hand spinning, and the machine allowed one worker to turn many spindles, so far fewer hands were needed.

4.
CBSE pattern

Why did industrial production in India increase during the First World War? (3 marks)

Model answer

British industry was occupied with war production, so Manchester’s exports to India declined; Indian mills supplied war needs such as jute bags and cloth; and new factories were set up — so production rose and Manchester never recovered its position.

5.
CBSE pattern

Mention three features of the jobber system. (3 marks)

Model answer

The jobber recruited workers from villages, received a commission for each recruit, decided who worked on which machine, and extracted money from the workers.

6.
CBSE pattern

When and where was the first cotton mill set up in India? (2 marks)

Model answer

In Bombay in 1854, by Cowasjee Nanabhoy.

7.
CBSE pattern

How did advertisements help in creating new consumers? (3 marks)

Model answer

Through calendars, labels and posters, manufacturers used images of gods, royalty and Indian women to give their goods trust, status and Indianness, persuading people used to hand-made cloth to buy machine-made products and appealing to swadeshi sentiment.

8.
CBSE pattern

Why did the port of Surat decline at the end of the eighteenth century? (2 marks)

Model answer

Because the Company shifted its trade to Bombay, Calcutta and Madras, its gomasthas bound weavers to sell only to it, and cheap British cloth ruined the textile trade on which Surat depended.

11

Frequently Asked Questions

Quick clarifications

1.

Did the industrial revolution begin in cotton?

Model answer

Largely yes — cotton was the first industry transformed by machines, because demand for cheap standard cloth was greatest and the processes were easiest to mechanise.

2.

Were machines immediately better than hand labour?

Model answer

No. Where labour was cheap, demand seasonal or varied, hand labour remained cheaper and more flexible, and it survived well into the nineteenth century.

3.

Who were the Luddites?

Model answer

Skilled workers in Britain who destroyed frames and power looms in the 1830s and 1840s, believing machines would take their jobs.

4.

What is a guild?

Model answer

An association of craftsmen and merchants that controlled production, prices and entry into a trade in a town.

5.

Why did the Company eliminate Indian traders?

Model answer

To control the supply and price of cloth directly: the gomasthas replaced the network of Indian merchants and brokers who had earlier bought from weavers and sold to the Company.

6.

What were chawls?

Model answer

Crowded tenement buildings in Bombay where mill workers lived, with little space, water or sanitation.

7.

Why was the Indian workforce seasonal?

Model answer

Because many workers kept their links with the village and returned at harvest time, so mills had a fluctuating labour supply.

8.

Which Indian industrialist set up the first jute mill?

Model answer

Seth Hukumchand, who set up the first Indian jute mill in Calcutta in 1917.

12

Assertion-Reason Questions

Choose the correct option

How to answer

(a) Both A and R are true and R explains A. (b) Both are true but R does not explain A. (c) A is true, R is false. (d) A is false, R is true.

1.

Assertion (A): Proto-industrialisation was production for an international market.
Reason (R): Merchants supplied raw material to village artisans and sold the finished goods abroad.

2.

Assertion (A): Machines immediately replaced hand labour in Britain.
Reason (R): Hand labour survived well into the nineteenth century.

3.

Assertion (A): Women attacked the Spinning Jenny.
Reason (R): It threatened their livelihood in hand spinning.

4.

Assertion (A): The gomastha system strengthened the weavers’ bargaining power.
Reason (R): Weavers were bound to sell only to the Company at a fixed price.

5.

Assertion (A): The port of Surat declined by the end of the eighteenth century.
Reason (R): The Company shifted its operations to Bombay, Calcutta and Madras.

6.

Assertion (A): The First World War helped Indian industry.
Reason (R): British imports into India declined during the war.

7.

Assertion (A): Indian industrialists faced free competition in Britain.
Reason (R): British goods had free entry into India.

8.

Assertion (A): Advertisements used images of gods to sell goods.
Reason (R): Such images gave products an aura of trust and divinity.

9.

Assertion (A): The jobber was a government official.
Reason (R): He was an old worker employed to recruit new workers.

10.

Assertion (A): Cotton was the first industry to be mechanised.
Reason (R): The demand for cheap standard cloth was greatest in cotton.

Source-Based and Case-Based Questions

Read the passage or table, then answer

Source 1 — Proto-industrialisation

Source extract

In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, merchants from the towns in Europe began moving to the countryside, supplying money to peasants and artisans, persuading them to produce for an international market. With the expansion of world trade and the acquisition of colonies in different parts of the world, the demand for goods began growing. But merchants could not expand production within towns. This was because here urban crafts and trade guilds were powerful. These were associations of producers that trained craftspeople, maintained control over production, regulated competition and prices, and restricted the entry of new people into the trade.

1.

Why could merchants not expand production within towns?

Model answer

Because the urban crafts and trade guilds were powerful: they trained craftspeople, controlled production, regulated competition and prices, and restricted the entry of new people into the trade.

2.

Why were village peasants and artisans willing to work for merchants?

Model answer

Because they were poor and eager to work for money; the merchant supplied the raw material and marketed the product, so the artisan bore little risk and needed no capital.

3.

What did this system produce, and what did it lead to?

Model answer

It produced goods for an international market in a decentralised, hand-based way — proto-industrialisation — and it led to the factory system, as merchants accumulated capital and a workforce accustomed to producing for distant markets.

Source 2 — The gomastha and the weaver

Source extract

The Company appointed a paid servant called the gomastha to supervise weavers, collect supplies, and examine the quality of cloth. The gomasthas gave loans to weavers to purchase new looms. But the weavers had to sell their cloth only to the gomasthas. They could not sell to other buyers. The gomasthas were outsiders and had no social link with the weaving villages. They acted arrogantly and often punished weavers for delays in supply.

1.

What did the weaver gain and what did he lose?

Model answer

He gained a loan to buy a loom; he lost the freedom to sell to anyone else and to bargain over price, since the Company fixed it.

2.

Why did the gomasthas’ behaviour make matters worse?

Model answer

Because they were outsiders with no social ties to the weaving villages, so they had no interest in the weavers’ welfare; they acted arrogantly and punished weavers for delays, which destroyed trust and cooperation.

3.

What was the long-term effect on Indian textiles?

Model answer

The weavers lost their bargaining power, many deserted their villages or took to agriculture, and together with the flood of cheap British cloth the system ruined the Indian textile industry.

Source 3 — Why hand labour survived

Source extract

In Victorian Britain there was no shortage of human labour. Poor peasants and vagrants moved to the towns in large numbers looking for work. There was no problem of labour shortage and high wages. Industrialists were therefore not interested in introducing machines that required large capital investment. In industries with a seasonal demand, such as gas works and shipbuilding, hand labour was preferred because machines would be idle for part of the year. In many trades, demand was for a variety of designs and colours, which hand production could supply but standardised machines could not.

1.

Why was there no pressure to mechanise in Victorian Britain?

Model answer

Because labour was abundant and cheap — poor peasants and vagrants moved into the towns looking for work — so machines that needed large capital investment were not always profitable.

2.

Give two kinds of industry where hand labour was preferred and why.

Model answer

Seasonal industries such as gas works and shipbuilding, where machines would lie idle for part of the year; and trades where demand was for a variety of designs and colours, which standardised machines could not supply.

3.

What does this tell us about the idea of “progress”?

Model answer

That technological change is not automatic or uniform: employers adopt machines when it pays them to, and the survival of hand labour shows that the industrial revolution was gradual, uneven and shaped by the cost of labour and the nature of demand.

HOTS and Competency-Based Questions

Think beyond the text

Higher order thinking

These ask you to apply, compare or evaluate. Model answers are indicative — your own well-reasoned answer can differ.

1.

“The industrial revolution was as much a social revolution as a technological one.” Discuss.

Model answer

Yes. The machines mattered, but the deeper change was in how people worked and lived: production moved from the home and workshop to the factory, work was regulated by the clock rather than by the seasons, and a new class of wage labourers emerged who owned no tools and depended on wages. Towns grew without sanitation, women and children entered mills, and workers organised in trade unions and the Chartist movement. The technological change would have meant little without these social transformations — and they were resisted, as the Luddites show. (Model answer.)

2.

Why did Indian weavers not become factory workers in large numbers?

Model answer

Because the mills that displaced them were few and located in the presidency towns, and the weavers were dispersed across thousands of villages; many returned to agriculture rather than migrate. The mill workforce was recruited through jobbers from specific villages, and it remained seasonal, with workers keeping their links to the land. Colonial policy also restricted Indian industrial growth, so there were simply not enough factories to absorb the ruined weavers — a contrast with Britain, where the displaced hand-workers moved into the mills. (Model answer.)

3.

Was the First World War a turning point for Indian industry?

Model answer

It was a turning point but not a transformation. British industry was occupied with war production, Manchester’s exports to India fell, and Indian mills supplied war needs — jute bags, cloth, boots — so production rose substantially and new factories were set up. After the war Manchester never recovered its old position. But the structural weaknesses remained: capital and technology were still imported, the government remained unsympathetic, and Indian goods still faced tariffs abroad. So the war opened a door rather than building the house. (Model answer.)

4.

Why did manufacturers use religious imagery in advertisements?

Model answer

Because they were selling machine-made goods to consumers accustomed to hand-made cloth, in a market where trust mattered and where the foreignness of the product was a liability. Images of gods and goddesses gave the product an aura of divinity and reliability; images of queens and emperors suggested quality and status; images of Indian women in traditional dress suggested purity and Indianness. Advertising thus did cultural work: it naturalised the new product and, in the swadeshi period, helped present Indian goods as national. (Model answer.)

5.

How does the chapter change the way we think about “industrialisation”?

Model answer

It shows that industrialisation was not a single event or a single country. It began as proto-industrialisation in the European countryside, took factory form in Britain, and reached India through colonial trade — first destroying the weaver, then slowly building mills. It was uneven in time (hand labour survived for decades) and in space (India’s mills came a century after Manchester’s). And it was always social: about who owned the machines, who worked them, and who bore the costs. (Model answer.)

6.

“The gomastha was a colonial innovation, but the jobber was its Indian echo.” Explain.

Model answer

Both were intermediaries who stood between the producer and the market and used their position to control workers. The gomastha was appointed by the Company to bind weavers to a single buyer, fixing prices and punishing delay. The jobber was employed by Indian mill owners to recruit workers from villages, taking a commission and controlling who worked on which machine. In each case the intermediary solved the employer’s problem — how to secure a reliable supply of labour or cloth — at the cost of the producer’s bargaining power. (Model answer.)

India: the mills

Chapter Summary

The whole chapter in a few paragraphs

Industry did not begin with the factory. In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, as world trade and colonial demand grew, merchants from European towns turned to the countryside because the urban guilds controlled production, prices and entry into trades. They supplied money and raw material to poor peasants and artisans, who produced goods in their homes for an international market — a system historians call proto-industrialisation. It was decentralised and hand-based, but it was production for the world market, and it prepared the ground for the factory.

The factory came from a series of inventions in cotton: Hargreaves’s Spinning Jenny (1764), Arkwright’s water-powered mill (1771), Watt’s steam engine (1781), Cartwright’s power loom (1785) and Whitney’s cotton gin (1793), together with the railway from 1830. Manchester became the centre of the trade. Yet machines did not immediately displace hand labour: where labour was cheap, demand seasonal or varied, employers preferred hand work, and workers resisted — women attacked the Spinning Jenny, and the Luddites destroyed frames. The factory brought long hours, low wages, child and female labour, crowded towns, and in time trade unions, Factory Acts and Chartism.

In India, the Company first intervened in the market through gomasthas, who supervised weavers, gave loans and fixed prices, binding weavers to sell only to the Company and destroying their bargaining power. Surat declined, cheap British cloth flooded in, weavers deserted their villages, and the revolt of 1857 further disrupted trade. But from 1854, when the first cotton mill was set up in Bombay, Indian industry grew — in Bengal, Kanpur, Ahmedabad and Madras — with industrialists such as Dwarkanath Tagore, Seth Hukumchand, Jamsetji Tata and G.D. Birla. The First World War was the great opportunity: British imports fell, Indian mills supplied war needs, and production rose sharply.

Industrialists also had to create consumers, and they did so through advertisements on calendars and labels, using images of gods, royalty and Indian women to give machine-made goods trust, status and Indianness. The chapter’s larger point is that industrialisation was uneven, social and global: it enriched some, ruined others, and arrived in India through the very trade that had destroyed its weavers.
